TWO GHOST STORIES. [Psom BRIHRLRIrs JOURNAL."] I.—CHE APPARITION.

" Store transactions of the Psychological Society began my Uncle Ralph, in that irritable tone he no well knew how to make irritating. "Two whole columns ! Are the men mad to publish such rubbish P If they put another word on that subject into the paper, I shall cer- tainly give up taking it." My mother and I received this announc unent with respectful silence. : It is an insult ton man's sanity to be asked to read , such staff. Talk about the advance of education ! indeed" (a hit at me for wishing to alt' ad some mathe- matical lectures). "In any young days people did believe such nonsense as that." "Why, Ralph, what in the matter ("ached my mother in that soothing tone which she always adopts when ! speaking to my uncle. " Matter !" he replied, looking at her angrily, as if she were in some mysterious fashion accountable for the freaks of his favourite' newspaper. "Why, here's a fellow come forward and declared that he has seen a ghost, and instead of putting him into a lunatic asylum, a lot of men have net together and solemnly discussed the possibility and probability of the whole cute' Idiots'" "Mutt one he an idiot to are a ghost!" : Idiot indeed, a raving lunatic !" said my uncle, ! angrily. My mother smiled quietly, as she said, morel as if she were speaking to herself than to as. "Yet Annie Won accounted a remarkably serod,lo woman:' Uncle gaded at her in astonishment. "Annie, what ' Anni- he inquired. "Your slater Annie, my sister Annie." What the deuce has sheto do with the Psychological Society r "Only this, that if all those who see ghosts are raving lonaties, she must In toe been one too ; for, to her dying days, she maintained that she had seen a —sell, a ghost, if you like the term." Porn ronment Uncle Ralph turned almo,t pale. I

believe the thought croe.. a his mind that my poor mother was losing her reason. Then, as she eat there quite calm and collected, he sprang up in one ef those Ills of passion which used to terrify me, but which now , merely excite mild amusement, for, as ona.nma says. it is only his may. He began in a voice which literally made our little mom shake. "Janet, how dare you insult the dead P" . . . . . but my mother interrupted him with the quietest of smiles. Ralph. Annie always said that she saw a sliest ; and it is you who inollit her. if you do not believe her. I never doubted her word, although I was with her at the time, and saw nothing. Dear Rauh," laying her hand I gently on his arm. "Do you linow that Annie's last words were. Do you remember, Janet, the morning that Edward came.'" Edward." Major Elliott repeated, as if not under- standing her, there mass touch of quiet amusement in my mother's smile as she replied, "Ye. Edward ; though you might well ask why not Fred, or Wil- loughby. Rut. please don't be angry. only eit down i quietly and I will tell you all ab at it. Iliad no idea but I that vou knew." When you went to India, twenty-five years ago next February. Annie was engaged to Edward Fortescue. You must have known him.—one of the beet and kindest fellows that ever lived. I believe 11C m. rehipped the very , ground she stepped on; and she, well in those days, at least, we all thought she cared for him. They were to be married in August ; and about the end of July he went down to Devonshire to spend a week with his , mother. How well I remember that time. How we were all planning, contriving and working at the trousseau, and how delighted Annie used lobe as each pretty new thing came home. New you remember our old room at Sutton. where . _ _ .

div.head: IL-AN UNDENIABLE ABPARMON.
div.p: IL-AN UNDENIABLE ABPARMON.

At a town in the West of England was held a club of twenty-four people, which assembled once a week to drink ponli, smoke tobacco, and talk politic. Like Itubens academy at Antwerp, each member had his V'ellrlar chair, and the president's was more exalted than the teat. One of the members had been inn dying gem° fe some time ;of course, his chair, while he at ;e; absent, remained vacant. . . .

Tine chib being net ni the usual night, inquiries were naturally made after their asswiate. An lie lived in the aiff.ining house, a particular friend went himself to inquire for him, mid returned with the dismal tidings that he could not possible survive the night. This threw a gin in on the company, and all efforts to tum the con- venation from tile sad subject before them were ! ineffectual. . . . . .
Almut midnight (the time by long preacriptinn appre, prigt,d f, the walkin4 speetrer) the rlrK.r open, d, aud it, fate the dying, m rather of the

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. AUGUST 24, 1889.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. AUGUST 24, 1889.

, dead, man, walked into the room, and took hi. seat in 1 the accustomed chair: there he remained in silence, ' and in silence was gazed at. The apparition continued a selS-loot time in the chair to assure all present of the reality of the vision ; at length he rose and stalked n.warls the door, which he opened as if living, walked oat, and then shut the door atter him. Otter a long pause, soin.ne at last had the resolution to say,. If only one of us had seen this. he would not have been believed, hut it is imp msible that so many persons can have b.s.n deceived." he company by degrees recovered their speech, and the whole conversation, as may he imagined, was upon the de adf ol object which had erg gni their attention. They broke up and went home. In the morning inqoiry was made after their sick friend—it was answered by an ...not et his death, which happened nearly at the time of las appearing in the club. There could be little doubt before, but Pnir nothing could tio mare certain th m the reality of the apparition, which had been seen by so many persons together. It is neediest to say that such a story spread over the country, and found credit even from infidels: for in this case all reasoning became superflorma when opposed to a plain fact asserted toy three and twenty witnesses. Ti: assert the doctrine of the fixed laws of Nature was ridiculous, when there were IVO noun people of credit to , prove that they might be unfixed. Years rolled on—the story ceasnl to engage attention, and it FM forgotten,unless when ocoisionally produced to silence an unbeliever. One of the clob was an apothecary. In the course of his practice he was called to ant old woman, whose pro- fession WAS attending on sick persons. She told him that Mt. could leave the world with a quiet conscienee but for one thing, which lay ,a 1 her mind—. Do you not remember Mr. 1. v, whose ghost has been so much talked of P I was his nurse. The night he died I left the room for something I wasted—lam sure I had not been absent long; but at ,ny return I found the bed without my patient. Ile was delirious, and I feared that he had thrown himself out of the window. I was . frightened that I had power to stir, but, after some time, to my great ast.ishment, he entered the moron shivering, and his teeth chattaring—lay down on the bed, and died. Considering myself as the ranee of his death. I kept this a secret, for fear of what might be done tome. Though I could contradict all the story of the ghost, I dared not do it. I knew be what had hap- ' (tenni that it was he /Orme f who had lieen in the club- room (perhaps recollecting that it wan Um night of meeting), but I hope God and the poor gentleman's friends will forgive me, and I shall die contented 1"

"The tpleen of Bedlam it the sit le of a story of frontier army life by l'aptain Charles King. It is published in clear roillable type, Rod handsomely bound, at the price of Ifs. 141., by Nlessrs. 4'. Warne MO Co. Captain King made a hit with his story " Dunraven Rancho" and vent have not the slightest. hesitation in saying that Ids latest novel will be equally popular. Ile writes of frontier life as one who is'native and to the manner born," and, although Ile does not crowd his novel with charac- ters, he takes good care that those he does intro- duce shall be creatures of flesh and blood. There is a bit of lighting, and a bit of love.making, and a bit of plotting, which all combine to make a thoroughly readable Ismk. The writer has cer- tainly a faculty for this class of work, and if he can only keep up tire interest as well as he has done in tire two volumes we have had the pleasure of read- ing, he is certain to make himself highly appre- ciated as an author and well known to the novel- reading public. The current issue It the Camelot Series, publishol by Mr. Walter Scott, is'' A Week on the Cotword and Merrimac Rivers," by Ifeno. Thoreau, with a prefatory note by W. 11. tricks. Those who had the pleasure 4:l' reading Thonou's "Walden,' published in this series, will not fail to possr,s themselves of the vein.) just itsued. Thoreau is or original as a writer that pulls the ordinary thinker up at almost every turn 'and gives him foist for reflection. He has a goal deal of ittlititlit knowledge and vet he is not a scientist, for he is, alsote an things, a phi4oopltie lover .4 Nature. Ho gets out on these rivers to be alone with Nature and with Ord, and gives in vivid language what he sees, and trots, and thinks. Of rivers themselves he says,'' Tiny Un Tey lit have been the guides which condueted the foitsteps of the Seat travellers ; they are a constant lure when they flow by our d.wrs to distant enterprise and adventure, and by a natural impulse the dwellers on their banks would at length accompany thoir currents to tins lowlands of the globe, or explore at their invitation the interior of , continents." We can cordially commend the volume before us as a oltillingsworth of literature of the very highest rank. . In tire'' English Nlen of Letters," published by Nletsrs, Slacinillan and Co., we have a" Life of Henry Fielding,l by Mr. Aostin Dohs.. div.head: TWO MEN KILLED AT BILSTON.
div.p: TWO MEN KILLED AT BILSTON.

While five men wens working on a scaffold fifty feet high at Spring Vale Works, Bilston, tin Tueralay, the scaffold collapsed. Richard Colley, aged twenty, fell on his head, and was killed on the spit ; and Thomas Jud- son, thirty-four, died directly after his admission to Wolverhampton Hospital. Thomas Bennett was terribly injorisl and is in a critical COTlditill.. Robert Colley sustained a broken ankle, fifth man escaped unin- jured.

div.head: TUE FORTH BRIDGE.
div.p: TUE FORTH BRIDGE.

At the hal &yearly meeting of the Forth Bridge Railway Company, held at Edinburgh on Tuesday, Lord Colville, who prodded, said that there were at presort 850 shore- totters in the company. The Forth Bridge was rapidly approaching completion. The great cantilever, were practically finished, and the rentral girders were being put into position. The directors hoped to be able to walk over the bridge in October, and if the approach hues were suffieiently advanced he thought they should be able to use the bridge for goods and mineral traffic early in 1890.

div.head: CHESIIIIIE MiItICIFLTITItAL SOCIETY.
div.p: CHESIIIIIE MiItICIFLTITItAL SOCIETY.

The annual show of the Cheshire Agricultural Society was held on Wednesday, at Congleton. The Society extended its area this year to live miles outside the borders of the county, and it was no doubt doe to this that the entries were much in excess of any previous year. The total number of entries was 584, as against 407 at the Chester show last year, which WIIP the largest since that at Crewe in 18,4 when the entries numbered 510. The attendance of visitors, in spite of the showery weather, seemed quite up to the average. In point of quality, the show was in some respects a better show than usual, and on the whole rather above the . ordinary high standard of the Cheshire Society. The • dairy cattle attracted a good deal of attention. The principal prize was taken across the border into Staffordshire by Mr. E. Simpson, Sidway Hall, New- castle. not wit [Wending the competition of the noted • herds of Tatton l'ark and Crewe Hall. The pair of dairy Cows exhibited by Mr. Simpson were objects of general admiration. There was a splendid turn- out of bulls. Mr. C. Sherwin, Ashley Hall, Altrin- chain, was first in the two-year-old class, and Mr. E. Simpson in the class for young bulls. The horses no a rule were of excellent quality, with the excep- tion of the class for cart or draught stallions under three years old, in which there was perhaps not a single thoroughly sound animal. Cheese is of course an important feature in the Cheshire show, and the judges inclined to the belief that in the large class it was of rather better quality than usual, and that in the small class it was not quite up to the mark. In both classes the cheese which took the first place was coloured cheese. The butter-making competition was watched with interest,but there seemed nothing new in regard to methods. With respect to sheep, the long-wools were perhaps the best class.. The Congleton Horticultural Society held its annnal show in a marquee within the grounds, and it proved an agreeable adjunct to the main exhibition.

div.p: THE MAYBRICK CASE.
DECISHEA OF THE HOME SECRETARY.

It was announced mt Thursday night that Mr. Matthews, the Home Secretary, had reprieved Florence Eii•beth Maybrick, and that the sentence has been c.ntnuted to penal servitude for life. We understand th at the official statement as to the &vision, if the thane :secretary declarwithat Mr. Matthews • has nodoubt whatever, after nvonsideration of the evid- ence, that the prisoner did administer the poioin, and with criminal intent, but that the conflict of medical evi- dence prohibits an absolute conclusion that the poison was sufficient to have caused death. Another correspondent writes —There is reason to believe that the ground im which the Home Secretary decided to commute the sentence in Mn. Maybrick was exclusively connected with the medical evidence as to the cause of death. That the prismer adminstered arsenic hi her husband with intent to kill hint is, in Mr. Matthew's opinion, clear beyond a shadi• of a donbt. that whether she actually succeeded in bier purpose in whither Mr. Maybrick, although suffering from the effects of the arsenic, might not, having regard to the general condition of his health, possibly have succumbed to natural causes, in not • clearly proved. The conflict of medical testimony on the point is inusirtant, and 'so is the fact that ot small a quantity of arsenic was found in the body. flat attempt at murder is actually proved, ac- cording to Hie Home Secretary, but the murder itself is open to the shadow of a linestion. Of this very at- tenuated dinffit Mr. Matthews luau given the prisoner the benefit. Among mentbers of the noise of Commons generally there appears to be a prevailing feeling of rit- fief that the woman is tot to be hung, though most of them think that she thoroughly deserved it. I believe that some of the members who signed the petition in , favour I commutation afterwards declared that had the Home Secretary on a fuller ronsideration of the eaSe de- ' tided that the sentence should he carried out, they would not haVe had a word to say against his decision. div.head: MRS. MAYBRICK%q PRISON LIFE.
div.p: MRS. MAYBRICK%q PRISON LIFE.

So many extraordinary sbcrics havc been circulated as to the life which Mrs. Maybrick has led sim7e being imprisoned that a few facie will be ro-ad with interest. Her present diet in very different to that she was first allowed, and now she is practically treated in the same manner as all convicted priscaters, but in reality she has not yet partaken of the food of the eonmmn lot. There ! jean bums-lon abroad that condemned prisoners are allowed to have whatever they like, but this is rod so. At the same titer their sctrrows am made lighter in nearly every instance by the kindly humanity of the medical gentlemen, who have the power to order what they consider neees!cary. In the present instance Pre. Hammond aid! Beamish decided that the prostration of Mrs. Maybrick consequent olvm the result of the verdict was of no serions a nature that she would require care- ful treatment and titter food than the regulations allowed. She was constituently put upon 't hospital allowance,- and up to the present her food has been supplied front the hospital. She has seldom spoken, but has read much. The con- demned cell is one of the debtor:s cells for first- class misdemeanants, and is a fae-Btndilr of the one in {Odell the Rev. J. Bell Cox was confined in the male prison. A curious coincidence is the fact that Mrs. Maybrick is tntended by the same two female wattle's who had charge of Mrs. Berry during her imprisonment, and up to the time of execution. They were allowed a holiday after their trying duties on that occasion.

On Monday night a collier named Robert- Hurst. aged thirty-one, of Wigan, was fouod deml on the London and North-Westiern Railway at ilindley Green. lie was lying ' 1111 the Inc.. With Ins head frightfully smashed, and it is supposed that when crAssing the hue he was knocked down by a pass- ing train. Near to him were forty yards of lilt- ing. usually used for snaring game, a.I the !opinion is that he was proceeding on a poaching ! expedition when he met with his death.

. .. An esteemed correspondent, Mr. is hexer WILMIANI, formerly of War- rington, sends Us a letter, Whial Wl' ri:l2 in another column, on "The polities! a." It 801,11 that he has his eyes open or the United States, 39 he had in Eii‘zi.rod, to everything in the way Of soda! and political evil. It is the nature of such men as Mr. Whithani to spy into abuses ; and sieiety is all the hotter for their watchfulness for hid as things are—and heaven knows they arc bad enough—they would he very much worse, if it were not that detectives are alwo-s on the tea-k of the children of' darkness. Our corres- pon.h.nt draws a terrilde picture of the corruption , and tyranny of the " Boss " system of polities which prevails to such a largo extent in the United States. The professional ptliticians appear to have it all their .iwn way, for they are organised, daring, and unscrupulous ; while—and it is the same everywhere —the "respectable " classes are onorganized and exceedingly timid. It seems almost incredible that a creature such us The Blind White Devil' described by Mr. Whithain should he able to blackmail everybmly who is seeking an appointment, or a coritract, or is concession ; hut so it is. Ile i•an make and un- make men, and they know it and, tinurons as they are. they yield to hint when they eight to light him. In a free country, people may be said p•t as good g.ivernors as they deserve. "'rho inachine" may for a tins,' mislead and swindle the masses, but if it keeps on doing it there is some- dung wrong with the manes themselves. It is true that some of the hest men in the United States —awn of the highest standing, intellectually and morally—hold aloof than politics ; they will not worry:mei soil themselves with the struggle ; and thus it happens that what is bad becomes worse. What is the remedy ? it will be asked. Is the !mistiest hopeless ? Not so, We ShOUR Say, IllthOligh no immediate improvmnent need be looked for. It is in the nature of things that when a Blind White, or other Devil gets the reins of government in his hands he drives faster and faster mi the 11.41 to destruction. until the pace is beyond him there is et millision and a smash; and the olevil either disappears, or he is " broken " and dungeoned. It was no with " Boss" TWEED of New Pork City, :end it will he so with "Boss" Ilisathry of San Francisco. Meantime, it is hard ti wait mail the crash miles; hut there is nothing for it but to light on and wait on. The hardest thing to bear is the concionsness that as SOOll as one fraud has licon exposed and punished another will have establised itself elsewhere. It is the same all the WOllll over. And what then ? Shall the Reformer cease to struggle with the powers of evil r Nay, rather let Inm fall to the more earnestly and manfully, folk using that within which " nnikes for righteousness," and remembering no EIND.rS,II. America's wisest son lion emphatically affirmed, that after all the world is upheld by tits probity of goml iamb

Wilkinson, referring, on Sunday, to the death of Councillor Jolley, of Warrington, remarked that a friend of the deceased gentleman • had said : -" I have known Mr. Jolley from a 1,4 ; and I never knew him to tell a lie." I"The sooner these nurseries of immortality are suppressed the better." This startling—not to say revolutionary—expression of pillion appears in a Tory emitmnporary of Saturday last. What can it mean—pulling eburehes down and paving the streets with the stones Or has that' P. iv been at it again—confounding" immorality" with " immortality" The "P. D." seems to he " in- I stituted" when he ought to he "inhibited.'

Derry Gaol seems to be a veritable " • Two prisoners under the Coercion Act have died •I soon after being discharged from it and now Mr. I Conybeare, M.P., writes to say that he is sutler- •ing from rheumatism and lumbago. the conditions , under which he is forced to live being insanitary ' and abominable. It was Mr. Wilfrid Blunt who I stated that it was Mr. Balfour's plan to subdue . his opponents by prison treatment : and it would , maim that he is carrying it out. But there will be a day of reckoning for him. Mr. Patrick O'Brien appeared in the House of Commons, on Wednesday, and gave an account of , the murderous way in which he was ',atoned by the 1 rish police when he went to inert Mr. W. O'Brien at Cork Railway Station. Ile was struck by at , least four constables, and twice rendered insensihle, although he was conducting himself as a pearable I I citizen. But all this is what Mr. Balfour would I appear to like, for he refused the inquiry which I was asked for,much to the dis;,nuit of the Opposition, land to some of the Government supporters. Mr. Parnell might well say the police " were sent about , Iwith the hmitements of the Chief Secretary ring- I Mg in their ears, and with the knowledge that ' everything they did would be cloaked up and lied diem in the House of Commons."

A msn nom 41 Willivm Edwanls, a Liverpool iron- worker, was vent to prison for fourteen days by the Warrington magistrates, en Monday, for having stolen a jaeket, value S. 7,1., from the shop-door of .lohn E. Robertson, tailor and draper, 22, Rutter- market-st. On Saturday evening prisoner went to a pawnshop awl offered • coat in pledge. The manager saw that it was a new one, and that a ticket had been taken off it, and he became suspi- clout, lie was about to send for a policeman when prisoner snatched up the jacket, and made off, lie, however, nut plump into the arrai of Constable Corcoran, who took him to the Bridewell. Austin Hake, a labourer, came to N amngton on Monday. Ile had a few glasses in the morning, but did not get drank, and in the afternoon he met two young wen, of que-dionable character, whom Ire treated to whiskey at the Roebuck. Later on in the day he went to the Police Station and laid a complaint against one of the women—Catherine Connolly —charging liar with having taken I4s, 9d. from his pocket. Connolly was arrested, hut denied having committed a robbery. On Tuesrlay she wan brought before the magistrates. when she mid that : Hake gave her same money. Mr. flarnett, who pre- : aided, said that the case waa one of suspicion, but an there was a doubt the Bench had decided to dismiss it. They had no sympathy for the prosecu- tor. _

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday. three females —none of whom were very advanced in year, though each of them had compiled a list of previous convictions—were brought before the! magistrates. Jane Hewitt and Mary Coyne were charged with fighting in the beerhouse of James Richardson, in Dint-nt., on the 12th inst. F.ach defendant accused the other of having instigated the fight, and their mutual animosity. had so little subsided that Coyne strenuously dented Ilewites statement that she was married to the man she lived with. That was Ilewitt's 10th and Coyne's 43rd appearance at the Court, and they were each , hound one IO keep the peace tor six months. Maria Baker was charged with drunkenness in Fennel-st., on the 10th not, and with making a ills- turbanee. and she was convicted for the 24th time, a fine of 10s. and COSLI being impokied. A BRUTAL PENSIONER BROUGHT TO BOOK.

At the Warrington Police Court, yestenlay,Sansuel Tynan, 26, Golborne-st., an army pensioner, was charged with having assaulted his wife, Rebecca, and his father-in-law and mother-in-law, William, and Mary Mitchell, on the previous day, lie was also charged with having been drunk and disorderly. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the prosecution, said the prisoner knocked the complainants about in a brutal manner; be must have thought that he was in the army again slaughtering his enemies. lie knocked down his father-in-law and knelt on him, knocked down his mother-in-law, and gave his wife two black eyes. Ile earned Ws. a week, and had a pension of a Is. a day. Mr. Browne added that his wife desired a separation order. Evidence , given by the complainants showed that the prisoner had behaved most brutally, lon the magistrates gave him the option of a tine. They hail. the Mayor said, thought of fining him nts. and co,s. Ind as,: perhaps, in that case it would be more difficult for the wife to obtain an allowance from him, they had decided to make the fine 203, and costs, or a month's imprisonment. div.head: WRECK AND LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: WRECK AND LOSS OF LIFE.

FrOM an early hour on TOPSday morning, a heavy gale from the north-west blew off the Liverpool port, preventing vessels from leaving the Mersey. A number of marine casualties are reported. Off Soothisirt, the fishing boat Onward was capsized, and Thomas and David Blundell, cousins, were drowned. The small vessel Sturgeon, iron Preston to Peel, was alias- , dialed off Fleetwood, the crew bong taken off by the Blackpool strainer Bickerstaffe. At Rhyl, the pleasure boat Kate, ownol by Mr. Perry, of Birkenhead, was capsirol shortly after leaving Voryd Harbour, Idly!, but the three Birkenhead boatmen mere rescued by a passing scluoner and taken into the Dee. The sloop Busy, which was abandoned roar Hilbre Island on Tuesday, did not become a wreck, but was subsequently boarded by her erew and floated. The schooner which was reported to be in a sinking condi- tion off the Great Ormes Head was succourisl by the Penmon lifeboat. A heavy gale again prevailed in the English Channel on VVednesslay.

BY TM BEY. B. NIGIITINCiALK.

RAINFORD PONOREGATIONAL Clll-11C11. Itainford, a large cliapelry "nays Baines, was vested in the Lot hems at a very early period." By intermarriage it came into the Stanley family, and the Earl of Derby is the present lord of the manor. I A writer of sixty years ago thus further describes it : --s Rainford, a elialielry in the parish of Prescot, ! hundred of West Derby. five miles N. from Prescce. Inhabitants 1,375. Tins place is remarkable for its excellent clay, used in the manufacture of crucibles and tobacco pipes to a great extent. The heretofore morass to the west of the township, called Itainforil MOM. has of late years been mild, improved by ! drainage." Enough this 101 be to identity the place whose Noncomformity is now to be traced. Canon Haines in Notilia Ceetrir.i. sap, :-- "The Chapel Llipi,enpall existed in the year 1577, and in the year lnfai woo stated to be six or seven miles from the Parish Church." At the latter date the minister of the Chapel was the

line. TIMOTHY SMITH, as we gather from the Parliamentary Survey for that year. I quote thenurom as follows: 4We do present that there is a chappell within Rainforth afforesaid, in the pish of Prescott, which is distant from the said PIO, Church of Prescott six or seaven statue myles, and from Sr. Ellen Chappell within the stil OA flour myles, 3tl poles to the myle 1 ' from Billing Chappell, in Wigan pish, three tnyles land a half, and from Holland Church about ffoure statue tuyies ; and there is not any houses of I (habitation) within two myles distance of the said chappell of Rainforth, but what (houses) are situ- , ate within the said serene of Rainforth ; anti that Mr. Timothy Smith lath now officiate as minister I them, and is the present incumbent there, anti , orthodox godly preaching minister, and came into I the said place by the consent oft lie chapellrie, and I fornily received for Ids sallary the same of fforty pounds p ann, allowed to the said ch glad' out of the sequestracons:' This Mr. Timothy Smith signs The Harmonious consent in 1644 aS minister at Rainford, and according to the docu- ment giving the names of those who composed the Lancashire Classical Preshyteries was here in 1046.!. Of this excellent man, who was afterwards ejected for his Nonconformity from Longridge Chapel, near Preston, tummy gives the following account • We. Timothy Smith, formerly minister of Bradshaw Chapoldhough lie did not conform.he often preached in the chapel after his ejectment ; for this being an obscure place with a small salary, there was no striving for it. Ile died very poor, in 1679, aged On.- There exists at Longridge a memorial to tilts good man in the present Congregational Church erected in /865. In Timothy Smith Ste have a pro- nounced Nonconformist,and be forms a good starting point in this history. At the time of the passing of the Act of Uniformity in 1662, the minister of Rainford Chapel was the

REV. EDGER BALDWIN. He also was a Nonconformist, and because of that was ejected from Rainford. Calamy also associates lam with Penrith in Cumberland, and gives the fol. I towing interesting account of him—" After his ejection he removed into Lancashire, where he took a farm, for which he paid a considerable tine. Hav- ing three children, he took it for their lives, not pat- ting in his own; hut it pleased God that he outlived them all upon which he spatted the farm, and at length fixed at Eccles, near Manchester, where be preached at Monks Hall, for many years, accepts ! ably and usefully. Ile was a solid, scriptural, judicious preacher; a man of good abilities, and of an agreeable temper. Ile was one of the Monday lecturers at Bolton. Ile died June 9, 1695, aged TB" Matthew Henry was greatly affected by the loss ot the " Roe, and learned Roger Baldwin, of Eccles; " and the celebrated Henry Newcome enters in his ' diary; —"June 13 116951 I heard of the sudden death of sir. Baldwin, of a diabetes ; and preached his funeral sermon. June 14th, on Matt. xxiv. 45, &e. It ion little difficult to explain Calamy, unless it lie that Roger Baldwin suffered ejection twice, which was no uncommon thing for these Noncon- formist worthies. Rainford Episcopal Chapel was honoured with a third ejected minister, the

which is the following inscription Here Iv.th with his wife and six children the Rev. Mr. Tetlaw. First minister of this place. lie preached in Role- ford near 43 years, and dyed December Ist, 1745, aged 19. In the graveyard: is also a tombstone in memory of Margaret Webster, one of Mr. Tetiaw's 11.ghterA, who died September 4th, 1771, at the age of 61. his successor was the

nEV. TATLoCK MATITKrt. lie was trained at Kendal by Sr. 111theeram, and came to Rainfonl in 1745. He remained here until his death --and was interred in the graveyard of the chapel. I copy in full the inscription upon his tombstone as follows: - The Rev. Tat lock Math, died the 23rd of August, 1785, aged 65. Ile was minister of this place abort 39 years. Margaret, widow of the Rev. Benjamin Mather,died Feb. 14th, 17:43, aged M. Alice, wife of William Julinson, ilied • Dec..ith, 1751. Benjamin. son of John Mather, I lied Oct. llt h, 1757. Sarah Mather elied Jan. 6th, 17114;* The oldest tombstone in the graveyard is to Richard Mather who departed this life ye 12th of Sep., 1724," I imagine: Mr. Tutlock Mather was a native of these parts, for the Mather family were numerous in the 17th and I.:th centuries in south and south- west Lancashire. Whether related to the New Eng- land Nonconformists of that name I do not know, hot suspect he was to the flee. Benjamin Mather, minister at Lower Chapel, Damns, from 17:1i to 1744. Probably :Margaret was the widow of the Barwen Slather, and mother or aunt of Mr. Tatlock I Mather, of Rainford. Thee

div.p: RI7. JAMES MIAMIAN!,

Ile is soil t;.11.1t1;71;;;"i;;;;"..; (lacking in the parish 01 Bolton. The Bradshaws for many gener- ations are associated with Bolton and district, anti titer are prominent figures in the great civil contest of the 17th century. Mr. James Bradshaw received Iris training in part at the Bolton Grammar School, and afterwards at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Calainy, who is our principat authority respecting these Nonconformist divines, says: d Through the influence of his uncle Holmes (a worthy divine in Northamptonshire) he left the University without taking any degree. Having pursued his studies for some time under his direction, he returned Mtn native country, fixed in this place fllindley, near Wigan] and there was ordained by the classis of which Mr. Earle was moderator; where he continued I until he was ideeted. In conjunction with many others, he had a concern intim; rising of Sir George I Booth,with • design to make way for the Restoration; for which he afterwards had very unsuitable ret urns. I After Bartholomew Day, Intkl, he suffered some i months' imprisonment for the crime of preaching. I through the malignity of a neighbouring justice suns own name ; but he was not to be frightened from his Master s service, or iliscounmed in it." After his ejectment he came to Bamford anti by "an ingeni- ous contrivance,- says Dr. Haller, he managed to retain the chapel for the Nonconformists. Calamy tells in the following passage how lie accomplished this. " When King Charles granted the indulgence," he says, " he removed to Rain ford, a consecrated chapel in Present parish, at a greater distance ; from his old neighbour, and there hold an ; amicable correspondence with several of the estab- lished clergy. who sometimes preached for him; ; which was one means of his keeping his chapel. 'the chapel wardens were obliged at the visitation , to make their app..aratice ;and he having a friend in ; court, the gli,thet was commonly proposed to them i in this manner: ' Have you eoMMOII prayer read yearly irs your chapels, to which they co std safely answer' Tes '; because once or more in every year, come of he neighbouring clergy read the service," lie had a urge family, and having but spoor chard • I was stir, in stronono4 eirciimstan,A. lie is Mii•l , to Imre inert frtspiently enneerlied in Ordinations. .. Ile was a liaol student, and a smart disputant ; . very lively in his family exercises, and over zealous I for the national interest and the public good." His death, which took place in 1702, in the 67th year of Iris age, was eaused by a bruise in his leg got by , riding during his preaching expeditions. A son of ' Mr. Ebenezer Bradshaw was pastor of the Dissenting / interest at Iltunsgatedn Kent. After labouring titers' S ; with great success he died and was interred in the , Sr. Lawrence cloirchyard. His tombstone contains ; the following inscription.-" Ebenezer Bradshaw, s I died March 11th, 1741, aged MU years." . ' " "

The onion of tice present Congregational Chorch j at Rsinford is thus accounted for by Mr. Halley. • After the Revolution," says he, 4. his [Mr. Brad- j thaw's] friends erected forhim a meeting house near j the chmml from which he had been ejected, and ' instituted a snit in the Duchy Court to recover the j endowments which had been given by the Preslty- terians for the benefit of preaching ministers. After prolonged litigation, they were compelled to resign their claims and to found a ihmentmg trust under the protection of the Act of Toleration." Bishop Gastrell,writ Mg of Rainford Chapel about 1720. says The onginall of this Trust was abt. Lad years agile, when this ehappell was recovered out of the Dissenter's hands, who had been in possession ever since ye warn." If. as Dr. Balky says. Mr. Bradshaw actually lived to see the new' chapel erected, he wan not permitted to labour ta it long; for as already stated he died in 1711 h, about the year of its erec- tion. Matt hew Henry in his 4liary writes .—"TI,., MI, day was a day of fasting and prayer, and imposition of hands in a very great congregation at Warrington, where, I trust, God was with on of a truth. I took the confession and vows, and Mr. Risley concluded with a serious exhortation. The work of the day was done to general satisfaction. There were many other ministers present." Before May. 1703, Mr. Tetlaw hail removed to Rainford. His congregation here would be considered one of the most important in the county, numbering 005 persons, of whom ffil were county voters. Mr. Tetlaw died at Rainford on the sth of December, 1715, after a ministry here of 43years. lie was buried probably in the aisle of the chapel where he had so long laboured.
